newsitem.title: USA: Glickman sees "more concilatory" debate on forests.
newsitem.headline: Glickman sees "more concilatory" debate on forests.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Thursday the so-called timber salvage rider had "polarized" the debate over how to manage the nation's forests, and expressed hope discussions would be more conciliatory next year.
"The salvage rider has been a real difficult thing, I will admit," the secretary said at a news conference reviewing 1996.
"I'm hopeful and confident that we will have a more conciliatory and productive public policy debate between Congress and the president on our forests," he added.

The emergency salvage rider, which expires Dec. 31, was passed by Congress in 1995 to speed up logging of dead and dying trees in national forests by reducing or eliminating many environmental reviews and opportunities for public comment and opposition.
Glickman repeated that he hoped to appoint a new U.S. Forest Service chief by the end of the year. The former top forester, Jack Ward Thomas, resigned this fall to take an academic post.
